articles.title: Natalie Nakase’s unlikely journey: a 5-foot-2 walk-on, coach in Japan, and now in the WNBA Finals
articles.summary: The Athletic has live coverage of Dream vs. Valkyries in the WNBA Finals Game 5. Every step of her basketball journey, there was a logical reason why Natalie...
articles.body:
The Athletic has live coverage of Dream vs. Valkyries in the WNBA Finals Game 5 .

Every step of her basketball journey, there was a logical reason why Natalie Nakase was unlikely to get a shot.

At 5-foot-2, she didn't have the profile (even as a walk-on) to play at UCLA. She played professionally in the shadows, competing for unheralded teams like the San Jose Spiders and San Diego Siege in the short-lived and now-defunct National Women's Basketball League. From there, she coached in largely unrecognized outposts, like leading the Saitama Broncos in Japan or the Wolfenbüttel Wildcats in Germany.

For Nakase, it didn't matter where she played or coached. Didn't matter if it was men or women. Didn't matter if there were big crowds or none at all. As long as there was a basketball.

Her gumption slowly opened doors. Her talent and vision of the game kept getting her to the next rung of the coaching ladder, landing on Doc Rivers' staff as a Clippers assistant before joining the WNBA's Aces with Becky Hammon and then being plucked by Joe Lacob as the Golden State Valkyries first coach.

"Hey, I wasn't that talented of a player, so? I think what I've learned is, no matter your size, it's really more your heart and your fight that comes out," she said. "That was to me something I really wanted to instill (as a coach)."

How fitting a mindset for the woman who has a second-year expansion franchise fighting for a championship, tied 2-2 with the Atlanta Dream in the WNBA Finals .

Nakase, 46, assembled a group of players — many of whom had been cast-offs — and molded underdogs into predators.

"I still wanted to bring another level of fight and confidence into them, because that's for me the biggest thing," she said. "You don't always have to be the tallest player. You don't have to be the fastest or most athletic, but if you have a fight in you, that never-quit type of mentality, I think you can go pretty far."

Those who witnessed Nakase's dogged determination along her journey learned not to doubt how far she'd go.

In the sectional championships at Marina High in Huntington Beach, Calif., a 5-foot-2 point guard dropped 27 points with eight assists. She was named the conference player of the year and graduated as the school's career leader in assists, steals and 3-pointers.

Marina's then-coach, Pete Bonny, saw her basketball premonitions at a young age. "She was always a play ahead of the game," he said. "'If we press here and get a turnover, then they'll take it out. Then maybe we can get a five count. If not, we're down. We'll shoot a 3 because we're down six and it's two possessions.' Stuff like that. She's just ahead of everybody by a little bit."

She earned a scholarship offer from UC Irvine, but not UCLA.

"I thought she was a good leader, but she was tiny," said former UCLA coach Kathy Oliver. Nakase and her dad visited Oliver's office and her dad mostly made a case for her.

"We already had one of the best point guards in the country, Erica Gomez," Oliver said. "So I thought, 'OK, she can come, but I don't have a scholarship for her.' So, she walked on her first year."

When Nakase tore her ACL, she impressed Oliver. And the experience likely shaped her as a future coach.

"She was a sponge. She watched Erica like a hawk. She was my little shadow. She'd follow me around when we were doing drills. She stayed by my side and was engulfed in the game. But she was a really good people-person. She got along with her teammates and was very observant," said Oliver, who coached Nakase from 2005-08. "I was thinking, 'What is this girl going to do? She's injured. She's tiny.' The next year, she worked so hard in rehab, worked so hard to get back. … Never count her out."

She became the Bruins' starting point guard as a sophomore.

"She was a great leader," Oliver said, "and so smart on the court."

After college, Nakase played professionally in the U.S. and in Germany, where another knee injury ended her playing career in her late 20s. She stayed in Germany and started coaching, and eventually was the head coach with the Tokyo Apache and Saitama Broncos — becoming the first woman coach in Japan's top-tier men's league, working there from 2010-12.

"Every time we had a road game, on the bus, she would sit down and watch film with me. She'd point out little things. She was really into film and brilliant on it. She pointed out things that most of the time, I didn't see, especially as a rookie," said John Flowers, a small forward for the Broncos.

Even with admittedly stubborn players, Nakase remained patient to get her philosophies across.

"I played for Bob Huggins in college. He has a specific style of play. I'm coming out of college, like this is how you're supposed to play basketball. This is the only way. This is the right way. I was showing her plays that we ran at (West Virginia). … She was telling me, 'That won't work here because it's pro basketball. It's a different game.' I didn't really listen. … I looked back and I was like, 'Damn, she was right this whole time. I should have just listened to it the whole time.' Three or four years later, I texted her: 'Man, I was such an idiot.'"

In the 2017–18 season, Nakase served as an assistant for the G League's Agua Caliente Clippers under Casey Hill, who had worked with her in Japan.

"It was a no-brainer. She was the first hire I made. I needed a very efficient coaching staff that didn't need a whole lot to be effective, and she was at the top of that list. It was pretty apparent from when we met — basketball means everything to her."

Her first scouting report together had already made an impression on him.

"It was like freaking nine pages long," Hill said. "It wasn't just like a blurb on each player. It was like a full paragraph. … I kind of knew from that point, this girl is going to figure out a way to make an impact in the world of basketball."

Hill and Nakase were later promoted to the L.A. Clippers' staff under Doc Rivers, where Nakase served from 2018-2020.

Nakase belongs to an exclusive sorority. She's one of 15 female NBA assistant coaches, spending 2018-2020 on the Los Angeles Clippers staff.

Jenny Boucek, an NBA assistant since 2017, recommended Nakase to her friend and Aces coach Becky Hammon, who had been the NBA's first full-time female assistant coach. (As part of the Aces staff from 2022-24, Nakase won two WNBA championships.)

Nakase was the first woman to sit on an NBA bench during Summer League. She is also the WNBA's first Asian-American head coach.

"Anytime you're the only one in the room, it takes a certain inner security, resilience and humility," Boucek said. "You're gonna deal with some stuff just from being the only one and being different all the time. There's a lot of battles that you can pick, or you can take it and learn and keep the big picture in mind. That's clearly what Natalie did."

As an L.A. Clippers assistant, Ty Lue was constantly challenged by his fellow assistant …. on the court.

"She thought she could beat me at one-on-one," said Lue, now the Clippers head coach. "We played every day, and of course, you know the results of that." Nakase would change some rules to gain an edge, but she never stopped trying to beat him. "Every day she wanted that challenge. She always wanted to fight and continue to keep playing."

Similarly, he noticed how she brought out that fight in players to get the most from them. He credits guard Terance Mann's progress from a raw rookie into the player who eventually had a series defining performance in the 2021 Western Conference finals.

"With all the film work, with all the player development, ballhandling stuff, how to read certain situations, she was really good," Lue said. "She kept saying, 'I'm telling you this guy is ready.'"

After three seasons as an Aces assistant, Nakase interviewed to be the head coach of the league's first expansion team in more than a decade. General manager Ohemaa Nyanin was impressed with Nakase's character, experience and expertise.

She was also impressed with Nakase's word choices during the interview.

"She let some expletives fly through the process. You know how like you go to an interview and you're on your best behavior? She showed me who she was from jump, and I just thought that that was really endearing because our athletes need people that are going to be open, honest, direct, kind, provide clarity, but also be authentic. … It didn't seem like she was auditioning for something. She presented herself as this was her calling."

Law Murray and Sabreena Merchant contributed to this report.

articles.title: El Real Madrid convierte el triple en un arma de destrucción masiva
articles.standfirst: Líder triplista en la Liga Endesa (15 por partido) y en la Euroliga (12,4), su arsenal ofensivo es un vendaval que no encuentra freno
articles.summary: Líder triplista en la Liga Endesa (15 por partido) y en la Euroliga (12,4), su arsenal ofensivo es un vendaval que no encuentra freno
articles.body: Este pasado domingo el Real Madrid trituró al iLERNA Lleida (86-122) para prolongar su condición de líder invicto y firmar un arranque histórico: 112,8 puntos de media en las cinco primeras jornadas de la ACB. Además, estableció un nuevo récord de triples en un partido, con 24 aciertos de 48 intentos. Detrás de semejante vendaval ofensivo está la mano de Pedro Martínez. El técnico ha inculcado su sello en tiempo récord: ritmo vertiginoso, circulación rápida de balón y una apuesta decidida por el lanzamiento exterior. El triple se ha convertido en una seña de identidad de un equipo que ataca sin descanso y encuentra amenazas desde cualquier posición. En la Liga Endesa, los registros son demoledores: 15 triples por encuentro y un 41,7% de efectividad. La confianza en el lanzamiento es tal que los blancos promedian casi tantos tiros de tres (36) como de dos (36,4). De los 16 jugadores que han participado, 14 ya han anotado desde el perímetro. Luwawu-Cabarrot, con 4,7 triples de media en tres partidos, lidera una lista en la que también destacan Maledon (2,2), Feliz (1,8), Llull (1,6) y Campazzo (1,5). Con tantos jugadores enchufados, las defensas rivales se ven obligadas a elegir entre proteger la pintura o conceder espacios a unos tiradores que castigan cualquier desajuste. La apuesta también funciona en la Euroliga, donde el Madrid lidera la competición en triples anotados (12,4 por partido) e intentados (30,7), con un 40,5% de acierto. Feliz (2,2), Campazzo (2), Okeke (1,8), Luwawu-Cabarrot (1,7) y Abalde (1,4) encabezan el prolífico arsenal exterior madridista. Una amenaza coral que multiplica las dificultades de cualquier defensa: cerrar una vía de anotación significa abrir otra. El potencial colectivo también se refleja en la competición continental: el Madrid es segundo en valoración, con 95,3 créditos por partido, sólo por detrás del Valencia Basket (99,1). Un dato que refleja la aportación de un bloque con muchos jugadores marcando diferencias. Eso sí, la superioridad que está exhibiendo en la competición doméstica todavía tendrá que ponerla a prueba en los escenarios más exigentes de la Euroliga. La maquinaria funciona, pero el verdadero desafío será mantener semejante nivel cuando los partidos grandes se decidan por detalles. Pedro Martínez mantiene los pies en el suelo pese al vendaval anotador de su equipo. “Lo estamos haciendo bastante bien en los últimos ocho partidos y tenemos que seguir haciéndolo igual”, advierte. Y resume su receta: “Nosotros tenemos que seguir nuestro camino, hacer nuestros básicos bien hechos, lo que entrenamos y confiar”. De momento, su Madrid corre, tira y aplasta. Y en la ACB, juega en otra Liga.

articles.title: WNBA Finals: League to hold Game 6 Thursday afternoon at State Farm Arena
articles.summary: The Dream have played all their home playoff games at State Farm Arena this postseason.
articles.body:
After days of deliberation, the WNBA has finally determined where and when Game 6 of the Finals will be played.

The league announced Monday the contest will be held at 12:30 p.m. ET on Thursday at State Farm Arena in Atlanta.

The decision comes after it was reported Sunday the league was unclear about both the time and place in which the game would be played, and was working with the Atlanta Dream, Golden State Valkyries, NBA and the Atlanta Hawks to come up with a solution.

In order to accommodate Thursday's game, the league opted to move it to earlier in the day. That decision allows both the Dream and Hawks to play home games at State Farm Arena on Thursday.

In a statement, WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert said the league saw the success of Games 3 and 4 and wanted to host Game 6 in the same arena.

"The sellout crowds and extraordinary atmosphere at State Farm Arena for Games 3 and 4 were a tremendous success, and we're excited to give thousands more fans the opportunity to experience Game 6 with a championship on the line," said WNBA Commissioner Cathy Engelbert. "We thank the NBA, Dream, Valkyries, Hawks, State Farm Arena and USA Network for the collaboration and flexibility that made this move possible. We look forward to delivering another unforgettable Finals experience in Atlanta."

Dream fans didn't hesitate after the news, either. The team said that 10,000 tickets were sold in the first 90 minutes that they were available on Monday.

The WNBA knew Saturday — when the Valkyries evened the series with a 67-62 win in Game 4 — that scheduling Game 6 was going to take some work. Throughout the playoffs, the Dream have played home games at State Farm Arena — where the Hawks play their home games. That decision was partially due to fan demand, as the Dream's current home stadium, Gateway Center Arena, has the smallest capacity in the league, with just 3,500 seats. State Farm Arena can hold 17,000 fans.

But Game 6 provided the WNBA with a major scheduling conflict, as the Hawks were scheduled to play the Cleveland Cavaliers at State Farm Arena on the same day and at roughly the same time as the WNBA planned to hold Game 6 of the Finals.

The Hawks and Cavaliers were initially scheduled to play at 7 p.m. ET on Thursday. The Dream and Valkyries were initially scheduled to play at 8 p.m. ET on Thursday. With the change the Hawks and Cavaliers will now tip off at 8 p.m. ET.

When asked whether the early tip time would impact the game, Dream guard Allisha Gray said it didn't matter when the two teams played.

"I mean, it's the Finals. You just gotta do what you gotta do. We're locked in on winning Game 6. I don't care if we're playing at 8 a.m., 10 a.m., midnight. We've got a championship to win."

Dream coach Karl Smesko agreed, saying shootaround might be affected, but that's it.

It wasn't the first time in the series the league had to change its scheduling. In order to work around the Hawks' schedule, the WNBA moved Game 3 of the Finals up a day and adjusted the time of Game 4 so both contests could be held at State Farm Arena. It was a successful move, as the Dream sold out both games at the stadium.

On Sunday, it was reported that similar options were on the table for Game 6, including the WNBA moving back the date of the contest by a day to accommodate both teams. That solution came with a catch, however, as it would require the league to also shift the date of a possible Game 7 to ensure both teams received adequate rest before taking the court for the game. Ultimately, the league found another solution.

With the Game 6 situation finally sorted out, the WNBA shouldn't have to worry about the issue again. The Dream will begin playing their home games at State Farm Arena in 2027.

articles.title: Thunder's Jalen Williams out indefinitely with fractured fibula, dislocated ankle after gruesome injury in win over Clippers
articles.summary: Williams and Cason Wallace could both miss the rest of the 2026-27 season.
articles.body:
Jalen Williams is headed for surgery and is likely out for the rest of the season.

The Oklahoma City Thunder guard suffered a fractured fibula and a dislocated left ankle in their win over the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday night, general manager Sam Presti announced. A specific timeline for his return is not yet known, and won't be until after he undergoes surgery.

Fellow Thunder guard Cason Wallace has a torn labrum in his left shoulder and is also headed for surgery. According to ESPN's Shams Charania , both players are expected to be sidelined for several months and will miss most, if not the entire, rest of the 2026-27 campaign.

Williams was taken off the court at the Paycom Center on a stretcher in the final minutes of the Thunder's 108-101 win over the Clippers on Sunday. He was fouled while going up for a dunk and landed awkwardly on his left leg, which crumbled underneath him as he came down.

The injury was gruesome, and a Thunder staffer quickly covered Williams' left leg with a towel as others rushed in to tend to him. Several teammates leaned over him, too.

Williams was eventually lifted onto a stretcher and received a standing ovation from Thunder fans as he made his way out of the arena.

Kris Dunn was called for a flagrant foul for his hit on Williams. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander took the free throws for him, and the game then wrapped up normally.

The injury caused a pretty emotional scene on Sunday, and Gilgeous-Alexander teared up during his postgame interview on the floor.

"I have no doubt in my mind that he'll be back and be better than he was before, just like how he handled the last couple of injuries," Gilgeous-Alexander said, via The Oklahoman's Justin Martinez . "It's unfortunate, his luck so far, but he's equipped for it. He's a warrior."

Williams played just 33 games last season due to various injuries, including a hamstring injury that impacted him during the Western Conference finals. Williams averaged 17.1 points and 5.5 assists per game last season. The 25-year-old is in the first year of a five-year, max $239 million deal with the Thunder. He had eight points and five assists on Sunday night.

Wallace, who also left Sunday's loss early with his shoulder injury, is in his fourth season in the league this fall. He averaged a career-high 8.6 points and 2.6 assists per game last season.

Now with Williams and Wallace out recovering, the Thunder will have to play at least the majority of the rest of the regular season without them. Sunday's win marked their third straight to open the year, so they are off to a good start despite the two major setbacks.

The Thunder will take on the Phoenix Suns on Monday night in their first back-to-back of the season.

articles.title: Russell Westbrook, Thunder Reunion Addressed by Sam Presti After Jalen Williams, Wallace Injuries
articles.summary: The Oklahoma City Thunder have been rattled by injuries already this season, and they'll likely need to add a player to the roster to make up for the absences.
articles.body:
The Oklahoma City Thunder have been rattled by injuries already this season, and they'll likely need to add a player to the roster to make up for the absences.

After Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace's injuries, general manager Sam Presti addressed a potential reunion with franchise legend Russell Westbrook.

"I haven't thought about anything relative to the roster spot," Presti told reporters (19:30 mark). "I understand the question, but all I'm really focused on right now is players, giving them the right support, and then helping everybody with our group."

Williams suffered a gruesome leg injury against the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday, and Presti announced Monday that he suffered a fractured fibula and a dislocated left ankle.

In addition to Williams' injury, Presti announced that Wallace suffered a left labral tear in his shoulder and will have to have surgery.

Both players are expected to miss most of the season. As a result of the injuries, Oklahoma City can apply for a Disabled Player Exception for both players.

Westbrook played with the Thunder from 2008 to 2019, winning MVP in 2017 and establishing himself as one of the best players in franchise history. He played for six teams after leaving Oklahoma City and announced his retirement before the 2026-27 campaign.

It's hard to say whether Westbrook would be willing to come out of retirement to join his former squad, or whether the Thunder are even interested in bringing him back.

While it would be quite the story, the OKC still has its eyes set on winning a championship, and the 37-year-old Westbrook likely isn't the best option to replace the offensive and defensive output of Williams and Wallace.

A more likely outcome would be for the Thunder to sign a younger player they can bring off the bench while counting on their starters to carry the load without Williams and Wallace.

articles.title: Jalen Williams: Oklahoma City Thunder star requires surgery for broken leg and dislocated ankle
articles.summary: Jalen Williams was wheeled off the court during the closing minutes of Oklahoma City Thunder's win over the Los Angeles Clippers; Shai Gilgeous-Alexander was among the players visibly upset by the injury to Williams' lower left leg
articles.body:
Williams - a shooting guard who entered Sunday having averaged 18 points per game in his first 250 NBA contests - has been an All-Star and an All-NBA player already in his career and was a huge part of the Thunder team that won the 2024-25 NBA title.

He injured his lower left leg and saw his ankle turn at an unnatural angle in a drive with 1:14 remaining, with Williams immediately treated by medical personnel after going down underneath the basket on the Thunder's offensive end.

"Dub, as everybody knows, is as tough as they come," Thunder GM Sam Presti said at a news conference in Oklahoma City.

"He's an elite competitor. Even last night, just miraculous in terms of his outlook and the way he's looking forward to attacking this. We're going to be with him the entire way."

Williams' ankle was draped with towels before a stretcher was brought out, with players left visibly shaken by the incident and the game stopped for around five minutes before the Thunder completed their victory.

"Just feel bad for him," Thunder guard Shai Gilgeous-Alexander said in a post-match interview, fighting back tears as he spoke. "Nothing more than that."

Williams, seated up on the stretcher, saluted the cheering fans with two thumbs-up signals as he was wheeled off the court.

It was a double gut punch for the Thunder on Monday, with the team also revealing that forward Cason Wallace will need surgery to repair a left labral tear after suffering an injury in the same game.

The timetable for Wallace's return will also be set after surgery, but such procedures typically require several months of rehabilitation. Williams was an All-Defensive team selection in 2024-25; Wallace was picked to that team last season.

"Tough night last night," Presti said. "There's no way to paint that differently. We say within our walls all the time there's a difference between being positive and being optimistic.

"Not going to sit up here and say this is exactly where we want to be or this is how we'd like to have it, but at the same time, we're extremely optimistic about the recovery for both the players. Most importantly, things could have been a lot worse."

The Thunder have experienced major injury-related challenges in recent years, including Chet Holmgren missing the entirety of what would have been his rookie season with a foot issue.

The team's 2024 first-round pick, Nikola Topic, missed all but 10 games in the previous two seasons - first because of a torn ACL, then with testicular cancer. And Williams missed 49 regular-season games a year ago with an array of issues, mostly wrist and hamstring problems.

"We've had some tough, uniquely tough, circumstances over the last few years," Presti said. "One of the things I tried to say to the staff this morning when I talked to them was we can't get to the point where we feel like this is a common situation. But that being said, it's our situation."

articles.title: Dwyane Wade Says Giannis and Bam Adebayo Need to Have a Conversation, Reflects on LeBron Pairing
articles.summary: Perhaps nobody in NBA history knows what it is like to be an established star in Miami and joined by another future Hall of Famer better than Dwyane Wade, and the Heat legend had some advice for Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo.
articles.body:
Perhaps nobody in NBA history knows what it is like to be an established star in Miami and joined by another future Hall of Famer better than Dwyane Wade, and the Heat legend had some advice for Bam Adebayo and Giannis Antetokounmpo.

"I want to see Giannis come down and say 'Hey Bam, I got this. This is my show, I'm going to make sure we all eat, though,'" Wade said on his WY Network by Dwyane Wade podcast (h/t Anthony Chiang of the Miami Herald ).

"Bam has been talking about Defensive Player of the Year and not getting the respect. I think this is the year Bam turns his attention to being the overall player in our league more so than 'We need Bam to score 83.' There's going to be some nights we're going to need Bam to knock down the [three] ball. There's going to be some nights we're going to go to Bam and he's going to lead this unit.

"'But, Bam, I need you to be a monster on the other end of the floor and let me handle all the playmaking and all the up and down.' Are they going to have that conversation? Are they going to look at each other and be like, 'Hey, it's my team, respectfully, but I'll make sure everybody else gets involved.'"

Wade was already an icon in Miami when LeBron James joined him ahead of the 2010-11 campaign much in the same way Antetokounmpo joined Adebayo's Heat this offseason.

While the assumption was the Heat would dominate the league behind the James, Wade and Chris Bosh trio, they lost the NBA Finals to the Dallas Mavericks that first season as they were still getting adjusted to playing together.

"We had this in Miami with Bron and I," Wade said. "Bron came, and I think it took us about a year before Bron could be LeBron. Him and I were back and forth. 'Hey, you shot two shots in a row.' And it wasn't like that, but it was like that. It was like, 'All right, I don't want to shoot too much. I don't want to do too much.'"

It's a fascinating insight into the early days of their Heat tenure together, and they eventually figured it out. After all, Miami won back-to-back championships the following two seasons, further cementing their status as future Hall of Famers and legends of the game.

Perhaps Antetokounmpo and Adebayo are experiencing some of the same things, as Miami is off to an 0-3 start and has been among the most disappointing teams in the league in the early going of the 2026-27 campaign.

They are both talented enough to eventually adjust and have the Heat battling for positioning in the Eastern Conference playoff picture.

But it may take some time, just like it did with James and Wade.

articles.title: “Ridiculous”: Journalists Weigh In After NBA Scheduling Conflict Leaves WNBA Facing Unusual Championship Celebration
articles.summary: The Atlanta Dream and the Golden State Valkyries are tied 2-2 as both teams pursue their first-ever WNBA championship. That means when the Finals return to S...
articles.body:
The Atlanta Dream and the Golden State Valkyries are tied 2-2 as both teams pursue their first-ever WNBA championship. That means when the Finals return to State Farm Arena after Game 5 at Chase Center, Game 6 could potentially decide the champion. However, an NBA scheduling conflict has left the league facing an unusual dilemma, with journalists now questioning how Atlanta will handle a potential championship celebration.

WNBA reporter Noa Dalzell did not hide her frustration after ESPN reporter Ramona Shelburne recently discussed the situation, calling it "ridiculous."

Sports anchor Reggie Chatman Jr. also shared a similar reaction, writing, "Goodness."

Their reactions came after Shelburne highlighted the logistical complications surrounding Thursday's potential series finale. With the Atlanta Hawks scheduled to host the Cleveland Cavaliers at State Farm Arena later that evening, even a Dream or Valkyries championship could come with an unexpected catch: the winning team might not get to celebrate on the same court where it clinched the title.

"Guess what happens if someone wins a championship after game six? They have to turn that arena over for the Hawks game. And so that championship celebration may not actually be on that court," Shelburne explained, as per an X post by Underdog WNBA .

She added that discussions were underway about whether the arena could be turned around in time for fans to celebrate on the floor, with a practice court emerging as a possible alternative. The WNBA Finals Game 6 is scheduled for 12:30 p.m. ET, while the Hawks-Cavaliers game has been pushed back to 8 p.m. ET.

"It's not a great option, but it's the option they've chosen, and none of the options were good," she added.

The scheduling conflict stems from the Dream's decision to move their home Finals games to State Farm Arena rather than their regular home venue, Gateway Center Arena, which seats approximately 3,500 fans. State Farm Arena, by comparison, accommodates more than 17,000, giving Atlanta the capacity to meet the demand for a potential championship-clinching game.

Games 3 and 4 of the Finals have already been played at State Farm Arena, drawing sellout crowds. So sending a possible title-deciding Game 6 back to the much smaller Gateway Center Arena would have presented a significant challenge for ticket demand and the league's championship showcase.

However, State Farm Arena was already booked for the Hawks' regular-season matchup against Cleveland on Thursday, October 29. But rather than moving the Finals back to Gateway Center Arena, the WNBA, NBA, Atlanta Hawks, and broadcast partners ultimately agreed to a doubleheader.

That arrangement leaves arena staff with roughly five hours to clear the court, remove the WNBA Finals setup, prepare the floor for the NBA game, and accommodate the postgame proceedings if the series ends in Game 6. The compressed window could become particularly complicated if the winning team needs time for a trophy presentation, media obligations, and a championship celebration with its fans.

So the question is no longer simply whether the arena can host two basketball games in one day, but whether it can give a potential champion and its fans the moment they have spent an entire season chasing.

articles.title: Three Takeaways From the Sixers’ Best Start in Seven Years
articles.summary: The Philadelphia 76ers couldn’t have asked for a better start to their season. In the last three games, they’ve had the perfect mix of drama, excitement, and...
articles.body:
The Philadelphia 76ers couldn't have asked for a better start to their season.

In the last three games, they've had the perfect mix of drama, excitement, and success. For the first time since 2019, the Sixers have started their season 3-0. These wins have come over some serious contenders, and they've given spectators a lot to think about.

Three wins in, here are three key takeaways from the 76ers' fantastic start.

The Sacrifice Talk From Media Day Is Already Showing Up on the Court

Before this season began, the Sixers Media Day had one word at its core: sacrifice.

The team understood that talent alone doesn't win championships. To get everything to work, players had to understand their roles. In his media day segment, LeBron James defines what sacrifice is to him and what it should mean to the team.

"If we want to do something special, there will be a collective sacrificing in a good way," James said .

It sounded good for the team to all be on the same page, but it looks even better on the court.

In the clutch win against the defending champion New York Knicks, the Sixers were all in on each other. Each starter ended the game with ten or more shots. This showcased a healthy distribution of the ball and shot attempts. However, the real story is in the other statistics.

Each of the starters had a handful of rebounds, assists, and overall hustle plays. There were other intangibles that showed their willingness to play for each other. On top of that, each of them shared an important mutual understanding. When someone got hot, they all understood when the time was right for everyone else to clear out and let that guy get to his shot.

With some help off the bench from Anfernee Simons and Kentavious Caldwell-Pope , the Sixers were able to pull out a hard-fought team victory against the Knicks to open the season.

The Cavaliers Comeback Showed Both Versions of This Team

In the 29-point comeback against the Cleveland Cavaliers, one thing became glaringly clear. When this team is in full sync with each other, they can run teams out of a game. However, anything less is detrimental.

Philadelphia committed 15 turnovers in the first half. They gave away nine in the first quarter alone. Although James had five of them on his own, a lot of the turnovers were miscommunications between him and his teammates. Jaylen Brown also contributed with his own three turnovers, and the Cavaliers took full advantage of each and every one.

The second half was completely different. Philadelphia cleaned things up, committing only two turnovers between two quarters. They also more than doubled their assists number. They turned seven into 17 assists as a team.

Outside of ball-handling errors, poor defensive execution kills the team as well. The 76ers play some of their best basketball when they're turning defense into offense. In the first half, Philadelphia was late on closeouts. They allowed eight offensive rebounds, and ultimately lacked defensive effort. Because of the lack of effort, they fell down into a 24-point deficit by halftime.

Yet again, things improved in the second half. The defensive intensity surged, and the Sixers had applied the most pressure that they had been all night. They kept the Cavaliers to only two offensive rebounds. Ultimately, they outrebounded them 23-20. They also came away with seven steals to the Cavaliers' single steal.

Ultimately, the Sixers benefitted from stringing together stops and turning them directly into offense. By cleaning up their execution, the Sixers were able to climb a 29-point deficit and turn it into a victory.

The Center Depth Behind Embiid Could Be a Fatal Flaw

The third game, against Milwaukee, raised a question Sixers fans can't ignore.

In today's NBA, the deepest team wins the championship. Teams like the Spurs, Thunder, and Knicks have bench units that can compete with opposing starters. The 76ers' starting five is just as good as any. However, how do they fare when those five guys aren't always on the court at the same time?

It's clear to see that the front office needs to find a suitable center to play behind Joel Embiid . Ariel Hukporti is out for the season , and Dominique Barlow will be missing more time with his lower back injury. This leaves Dean Wade , Jabari Walker , and Adem Bona , who is playing through a foot sprain, left for the center rotations. Wade and Walker sit at 6-foot-9 and 6-foot-7.

This forces the Sixers to run small-ball lineups every time Embiid sits. Although they came away with the win against the Bucks, the Sixers were outrebounded 62-40 . Against a better team, that gap becomes a much bigger problem. The small-ball lineups won't work against every team. They just haven't faced one that can capitalize yet.

Wins are to be celebrated of course, but such a glaring issue demands a bigger question. Philadelphia might have enough to help them survive one or two games, but the question of if this playstyle will be sustainable come post-season is valid. On top of that, whether or not they can contribute to winning basketball come May-June is completely up to rotations at the center position.

A well-put-together starting five can sometimes get NBA fans across the world to jump in excitement about their teams prematurely. If the Sixers can take all the positives from their (now) 3-1 start and incorporate more executional habits, as well as explore some rotational depth at the center position, Sixers fans would be right to start thinking about a parade down Broad Street.

articles.title: Alex Caruso injury update: OKC Thunder guard out vs. Suns with sprained ankle
articles.summary: Alex Caruso will not return to OKC's home game against Phoenix on Monday due to a right ankle sprain.
articles.body:
Alex Caruso will not return to OKC's home game against Phoenix on Monday due to a right ankle sprain.

Caruso elevated to contest a jumper by Dillon Brooks at the 1:34 mark of the second quarter and landed wrong on said ankle, tweaking it in the process. He then limped into the locker room for further evaluation.

OKC has been hit hard by injuries recently . Cason Wallace tore his labrum in his left shoulder during a home win over the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday, and Jalen Williams also fractured his fibula and dislocated his ankle on the left side. Timelines for both players will be announced after they undergo surgery.

But the Thunder still got off to a strong start against the Suns thanks in large part to Caruso, who competed with his usual intensity on both ends. He recorded nine points, three assists and two rebounds in nine minutes off the bench prior to his departure.

OKC holds a 67-53 lead over Phoenix at halftime.

articles.title: Sergio de Larrea se lesiona y abandona el partido a los seis minutos de juego
articles.standfirst: El base español tuvo que irse a vestuarios por una distensión en la rodilla derecha tras una acción con Tim Hardaway Jr
articles.summary: El base español tuvo que irse a vestuarios por una distensión en la rodilla derecha tras una acción con Tim Hardaway Jr
articles.body: Tras la primera gran noche que vivió en uno de sus primeros partidos como recién llegado a la NBA, Sergio de Larrea ha sufrido también de manera anticipada un contratiempo. El base tuvo que abandonar la cancha de los Miami Heat cuando apenas había disputado seis minutos de juego. En una acción a los dos minutos de comenzar el segundo cuarto, un choque con Tim Hardaway Jr. ha dejado fuera del encuentro al 'rookie' de los Mavericks. Después de quedarse un rato en el suelo dolorido, de Larrea encaró el túnel de vestuarios con una cierta cojera y acompañado por varios integrantes del 'staff' médico. En el descanso, se comunicó que Sergio de Larrea tendría difícil regresar al encuentro tras una "distensión en su rodilla derecha". El español cayó al parquet tras el impacto con el escolta de los Heat cuando se disponía a recibir de fondo para subir el balón. Lo que parecía en un primer momento un golpe contra el suelo elevó su gravedad tras las pruebas realizadas dentro del vestuario. En el tiempo que había estado en pista, de Larrea sólo había podido coger un rebote y probar un lanzamiento de dos forzado que no tocó aro. Este percance puede suponer otro cambio en la progresión del ex de Valencia Basket, que en apenas una semana de competición ya ha vivido varias de las caras que ofrece la NBA.

articles.title: Giannis Outdueled by Cooper Flagg in Heat vs. Mavs, Box Score Stats, Highlights for Bam, Kyrie, More
articles.summary: The Miami Heat are still winless after four games.
articles.body:
The Miami Heat are still winless after four games.

The Heat dropped Monday's contest to the Dallas Mavericks, 113-109, despite a triple-double from Giannis Antetokounmpo.

The Mavs led 111-109 with under 30 seconds to play, and Andrew Wiggins' go-ahead shot attempt was blocked by Cooper Flagg. From there, Flagg helped seal the win on the other end with a layup to put Dallas up by four with just 10 seconds to play.

Antetokounmpo stuffed the stat sheet with a triple-double, but he also had quite the highlight reel, including a poster dunk against Daniel Gafford.

Unfortunately for Miami, Antetokounmpo's strong night wasn't enough with his teammates doing very little.

Cooper Flagg is off to a strong start to his second NBA season, and that continued on Monday as he displayed his passing ability while also getting things done on defense.

The 19-year-old is looking even more complete in Year 2, which is good news for the Mavs, but bad news for the rest of the league.

Kyrie Irving, still ramping back up from missing all of the 2025-26 season, also put together a solid night in the win.

It's hard to pinpoint exactly what has gone wrong for the Heat early on this season. They came into the year as Finals hopefuls, but have looked more like a lottery team through the first few games.

It is, perhaps, just early kinks that will get solved as the year goes on, but regardless, starting the year 0-4 is not a great look.

articles.title: Valkyries Beat Dream in WNBA Finals Game 5, Box Score Stats, Highlights for Angel Reese, Top Players
articles.summary: The Golden State Valkyries will have the advantage in the WNBA Finals against the Dream as the series tilts back to Atlanta this week.
articles.body:
The Golden State Valkyries will have the advantage in the WNBA Finals against the Dream as the series tilts back to Atlanta this week.

The Valkyries downed Angel Reese and the Dream 64-55 on Monday to take a 3-2 series lead and put Atlanta on the brink of elimination.

While nobody lit up the box score for the Valkyries, center Kiyah Stokes led the way for most of the night, with Veronica Burton holding things down in the backcourt.

Reese did her part on the defensive end with 15 boards, but she couldn't get much going on offense, shooting a lackluster 2-of-8 from the field.

Rhyne Howard led the way on offense, but her 20 points weren't enough on a rough night overall from the offense.

Game 5 wasn't a completely dominant win for the Valkyries, but there was never much of a doubt as they managed to hold off any attempt at a comeback from the Dream.

It was a rough offensive night for both teams, but more so for Atlanta, which shot 29 percent from the field, 23 percent from deep and turned the ball over 15 times. Golden State was slightly better, shooting 39 percent from the field, 25 percent from deep and committing just seven turnovers.

Atlanta seemed to have the momentum after winning Games 2 and 3, but it quickly went back to Golden State after a win in Game 4 and another victory on Monday.

Now, the Valkyries have the chance to close things out on the road on Thursday.

articles.title: WNBA Finals: Kiah Stokes, Valkyries shut down Dream in Game 5 to get within a win of first championship

articles.body: The Golden State Valkyries are just a win away from their first WNBA title.The Valkyries shut down Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream on Monday night in Game 5 of the WNBA Finals. They secured a tough 64-55 win over the Dream at the Chase Center, which gives them a 3-2 lead in the series ahead of Game 6 on Thursday in Georgia. If the Valkyries can win once more and secure a WNBA title, it would be a remarkable feat considering this is just the franchise's second season.Neither team shot well in the first half on Monday night. They combined to shoot just 5 of 29 from behind the arc in the first 20 minutes, and the Valkyries made only a single field goal in the final seven minutes of the game. But they managed to hold the Dream to just eight points in the second quarter, which allowed them to maintain a narrow three-point lead at the break, 25-22.Reese missed a good chunk of the first half, too, after she picked up two fouls early. But she still entered the locker room with five points and 10 rebounds. The 47 combined points made it the lowest-scoring first half in WNBA Finals history.The offense picked up in the third quarter, but neither team was able to separate much. Kiah Stokes was a dominant force inside and out through the first three quarters. The Eastern Iowa native helped shut down Reese inside and picked up three blocks while leading the Valkyries with a pair of 3-pointers. The 3-point bucket, her third of the night, gave the Valkyries a 10-point lead, their largest of the game at the time.That was part of a 16-6 burst to start the final quarter, and the Dream never got close enough to make a real push again. Golden State held on the rest of the way to secure the nine-point win.Rhyne Howard led the Dream with 20 points and five rebounds. The contest will be held at State Farm Arena, something that was once again in doubt, but will have to tip off at 12:30 p.m. local time to make it work. The Dream sold 10,000 tickets in the first 90 minutes they were available on Monday, so Atlanta fans are sure to show out once again despite it being a potentially series-sealing matinee contest.But it's going to take a much better offensive night to keep their hopes of a title, something the franchise has yet to win, alive.

articles.title: 'Stand or hide in the tunnel' for the anthem, Valkyries WNBA fans show loyalty; ready for early Finals Game 6
articles.summary: Golden State Valkyries fans face a 9:30 a.m. PT tipoff for WNBA Finals Game 6 in Atlanta due to Hawks scheduling conflicts at State Farm Arena.
articles.body: Caffeine might not even be needed. Pure adrenaline could get the job done. Fans of the Golden State Valkyries are in for an early-morning wakeup call on Thursday when Game 6 of the WNBA Finals tips off in Atlanta at 9:30 a.m. Pacific time. But during Monday’s Game 5 against Atlanta, which began like every other Finals game, with both teams leaving the floor moments before the playing of the national anthem only to return seconds after it completed, the packed Chase Center in San Francisco was raucous. Fans of this 2-year-old team, clad floor to rafters in their giveaway lavender T-shirts, were beyond keyed up. They were loud and on the edge of their seats, willing their team on every play en route to a 64-55 victory that gave Golden State a 3-2 lead in the best-of-seven series. That buzz could last a few days, which will come in handy when that alarm clock rings. WNBA FINALS GAME 6, A POTENTIAL TITLE-CLINCHER, WILL BE HELD IN THE AFTERNOON ON THURSDAY "I will be taking time off of work that day, for sure," one female fan said, planning a personal day for Thursday. "It’s really disappointing that more fans won’t be able to be cheering for the Valkyries on the West Coast," said another female fan, who brings her kids to games. "It’s pretty hard to do with kid drop-offs and school, but I’m going to make it work somehow." Some retirees said they get up early anyway, so they’re not sweating it and will be glued to their TVs for a road game, per usual. A couple of male fans said they would be watching on their laptops … at work. Shhhhhhh. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! The strange start time in Atlanta is due to conflicts at State Farm Arena. The Dream, who normally play at Gateway Center Arena, have played playoff games at State Farm Arena because Gateway has a capacity of only 3,500 for basketball games. But now that the NBA season has started, State Farm, home of the Atlanta Hawks, has gotten busy. Some juggling was required once it became clear that the WNBA Finals would be going back to Atlanta for a Game 6 on Thursday. There is a Hawks home game that night. Several other options were considered before the early game time was chosen to create an unusual doubleheader of sorts. Many fans in the Bay Area seemed far more concerned about the scheduling chaos for Game 6 than they are about the controversy surrounding the national anthem walkouts that have been swirling around the WNBA Finals since Game 1. "I don’t understand why we’re singing the national anthem [before games] to begin with, that’s all there is to it," one female fan said. "If they want to go back [in the tunnel] and re-group, great. We’ve been doing it for two seasons." CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE "This is a non-controversy that people are trying to make into a controversy," a male fan said. "I don’t think not being out on the floor for the national anthem says anything about patriotism or loyalty to the United States." WNBA ANTHEM CONTROVERSY SPARKS CALLS TO BAR PLAYERS WHO DON'T STAND FROM TEAM USA'S OLYMPIC ROSTER Many fans said that being on the court for the national anthem should be a personal choice for athletes, even if that isn’t the choice they would make for themselves. "We have strong feelings about this," said a female fan who came to the game with her husband and both were dressed from head to toe in Valkyries lavender. "We’re both retired military. So we stand, we put our hands on our hearts and we honor the flag. The players … are doing something to get ready for the game. WNBA SILENT AFTER FINALS TEAMS SKIP NATIONAL ANTHEM DESPITE RULE REQUIRING PLAYERS TO STAND AND LINE UP "It’s not new to us that they leave the court for the national anthem. If they stayed and saluted the flag [during the anthem], I’d be fine with that [too]. This country is so divided anyway. Everyone just has to support their own true feelings." There is actually a provision in the WNBA rulebook stating that players should stand respectfully on the court while the national anthem is being played. But the league has not enforced that rule since 2017. "I wish they would stand out there for the national anthem," one female fan said. "But it’s one of those ‘to each their own’ [things] and they’ve been doing it from the beginning. "Maybe the national anthem means different things for different people. articles.title: New NBA Rumors Reveal 2 Potential Kevin Porter Jr. Landing Spots After Bucks Release
articles.summary: Kevin Porter Jr. is reportedly generating interest from multiple potential suitors after the Milwaukee Bucks waived him before the season.
articles.body:
Kevin Porter Jr. is reportedly generating interest from multiple potential suitors after the Milwaukee Bucks waived him before the season.

NBA insiders Marc Stein and Jake Fischer reported Monday that the Denver Nuggets and Sacramento Kings are among those teams who "are still evaluating their respective backcourts and" could be interested.

Stein and Fischer added that Porter remains "optimistic" he will have an opportunity to remain in the NBA even though "finding a new home will not be immediate" since he is "not close to two-way eligibility" as a 2019 draftee.

Porter entered the league as a first-round pick in that draft and has played for the Cleveland Cavaliers, Houston Rockets, Los Angeles Clippers and Bucks throughout his career.

He has averaged double-digit scoring totals in every season of his career, including in 2025-26 when he posted 17.4 points, 7.4 assists, 5.2 rebounds and 2.2 steals a night while shooting 46.5 percent from the field and 32.2 percent from deep.

However, Porter appeared in just 38 games last season as he dealt with a right knee injury that eventually required surgery .

Still, it isn't surprising teams are interested after he finished with numbers like that, even if they came in limited appearances.

Sacramento could also use the backcourt depth with Ben Simmons out for the season because of a torn Achilles . Porter could, in theory, help anchor the second unit alongside Malik Monk and provide another high-scoring guard when Darius Acuff Jr. comes out of games.

As for the Nuggets, they could use more scoring outside of Nikola Jokić and Jamal Murray. They are the only ones on the team averaging better than 13.5 points per game in the early going this season and often have to do much of the heavy lifting on the offensive side.

Porter also won't cost any draft capital in return like he may have in a trade, so one of these teams could jump at the chance to add him in the future.

articles.title: Golden State defense stifles Atlanta as Valkyries move within 1 win of WNBA title
articles.summary: Kiah Stokes finished with a personal 2026 postseason-best 13 points to go with eight rebounds, three blocks and suffocating defense on Dream star Angel Reese, who was held to seven points.
articles.body: Kiah Stokes added three 3-pointers to a dominant defensive effort, Gabby Williams triggered a fourth-quarter run with a three-point play and the Golden State Valkyries grabbed a 3-2 lead in the best-of-seven WNBA Finals with a 64-55 victory over the Atlanta Dream on Monday in San Francisco. The 2025 expansion team will have an opportunity to secure its first championship banner when Game 6 is played Thursday afternoon in Atlanta. In a contest that featured the lowest-scoring first half in WNBA postseason history and threatened all-time record lows for total points by one and both teams in Finals history, the Valkyries led just 46-42 in the first minute of the final period before gradually pulling away. Williams ignited a 16-4 spree when she turned a drive to the hoop into a three-point play and a seven-point lead with 9:08 remaining. Stokes, a three-time champion who had made a total of just four 3-pointers in her previous 54 playoff games, then delivered the dagger with her third perimeter hoop of the game, creating a 10-point difference at the 7:21 mark. The Dream, who shot 29.2% overall and just 23.1% (6 of 26) on 3-point attempts for the game, got no closer than nine after that. Stokes finished with a personal 2026 postseason-best 13 points to go with eight rebounds, three blocks and suffocating defense on Dream star Angel Reese, who was held to seven points on 2-for-8 shooting. By running her streak to six consecutive games with at least three blocks, Stokes matched the WNBA postseason record set by Lisa Leslie in 2003. Veronica Burton matched Stokes' team-high scoring total with 13 points, while Tiffany Hayes and Cecilia Zandalasini chipped in with 12 apiece and Williams had nine. Burton also found time for eight rebounds and four blocks for Golden State, which won despite shooting 39.3% overall and 25% (6 of 24) from deep. Her block total matched Diana Taurasi (2009) for the WNBA Finals single-game record by a guard. Rhyne Howard was the game's leading scorer with 20 points for Atlanta, which, like Golden State, has never won a WNBA title. Jordin Canada had 12 points and Allisha Gray had 10 for the Dream, while Reese snatched 15 rebounds and Naz Hillmon pulled down 11. Atlanta's scoring total was just eight points higher than the all-time WNBA Finals low, set by the New York Liberty in a 59-47 loss to the Houston Comets in Game 3 of the 1999 Finals. The defensive tone was present from the opening tip. The teams shot a cumulative 18-for-67 (26.9%) and totaled just five successful 3-pointers in 29 tries (17.2%) as Golden State took a 25-22 lead through 20 minutes. Getting one trey apiece from Burton as well as reserves Kayla Thornton and Zandalasini, the Valkyries used a 3-2 edge in 3-pointers to create the margin of their halftime lead.

articles.title: Las Valkyries frenan Angel Reese y se ponen a un triunfo de ganar la WNBA
articles.standfirst: La defensa de las locales volvió a marcar la diferencia en un encuentro en el que limitó a Atlanta a un 29,2% de acierto y dejó a Angel Reese en 7 puntos
articles.summary: La defensa de las locales volvió a marcar la diferencia en un encuentro en el que limitó a Atlanta a un 29,2% de acierto y dejó a Angel Reese en 7 puntos
articles.body: Las Golden State Valkyries ganaron 64-55 a las Atlanta Dream en San Francisco y tomaron ventaja de 3-2 en las Finales de la WNBA, para situarse a una victoria del primer título de su historia. La defensa de las locales volvió a marcar la diferencia en un encuentro en el que limitó a Atlanta a un 29,2% de acierto en tiros de campo y dejó a Angel Reese en 7 puntos, con dos canastas en ocho intentos. Kiah Stokes y Veronica Burton lideraron a Golden State con 13 puntos cada una. Stokes añadió ocho rebotes y tres tapones, con cinco aciertos en seis tiros, incluidos tres triples, mientras que Burton aportó ocho rebotes, tres asistencias y cuatro tapones. Tiffany Hayes y la italiana Cecilia Zandalasini sumaron 12 puntos cada una. Gabby Williams terminó con nueve puntos, seis rebotes y tres robos, pese a convertir solo tres de sus catorce tiros. En Atlanta, Rhyne Howard fue la máxima anotadora con 20 puntos, seguida por Jordin Canada, con doce, y Allisha Gray, con diez. Reese capturó quince rebotes y repartió cinco asistencias, pero volvió a sufrir para anotar tras quedarse en ocho puntos en el cuarto partido. Las Valkyries llegaron al descanso con una mínima ventaja de 25-22, después de una primera mitad de dificultades ofensivas para ambos equipos. Golden State terminó con nueve robos y nueve tapones, y cometió siete pérdidas frente a las quince de Atlanta, una diferencia decisiva para encarrilar su segunda victoria consecutiva. El sexto partido se disputará este jueves a las 12.30 hora local de Atlanta en el State Farm Arena, según anunció este lunes la WNBA. La decisión generó polémica por situar un encuentro que puede decidir el título en plena jornada laboral, a las 9.30 de la mañana en California.

articles.title: Los Mavericks de Cooper Flagg dan otro disgusto a Antetokounmpo

articles.summary: Cooper Flagg lideró a los Mavericks con 29 puntos, 6 rebotes, 11 asistencias, 4 robos y 2 tapones
articles.body: Los Dallas Mavericks ganaron por 109-113 a los Miami Heat, que acumulan cuatro derrotas en cuatro partidos en la era de Giannis Antetokounmpo, en una noche en la que el español Sergio de Larrea se retiró en el segundo cuarto por una lesión en la rodilla derecha. Antetokounmpo firmó un triple-doble de 29 puntos, 15 rebotes y 11 asistencias, y fue protagonista con un espectacular mate ante Daniel Gafford, pero su actuación no evitó otro disgusto a Miami, que sigue sin conocer la victoria desde la llegada del griego. Cooper Flagg lideró a los Mavericks con 29 puntos, 6 rebotes, 11 asistencias, 4 robos y 2 tapones. P.J. Washington aportó veinte puntos, con cuatro triples, y nueve rebotes, mientras que Kyrie Irving sumó dieciocho puntos, seis rebotes y seis asistencias. Desde el banquillo, Walter Clayton Jr. contribuyó con quince puntos, tras convertir seis de sus siete lanzamientos de campo, incluidos sus dos intentos desde el perímetro. En Miami, Davion Mitchell apoyó a Antetokounmpo con 21 puntos. Andrew Wiggins y Pelle Larsson añadieron doce cada uno, mientras que Bam Adebayo se quedó en ocho, con tres aciertos en diez tiros. Los Heat afrontaron el último cuarto con ventaja de 84-83, pero Dallas se impuso por 25-30 en ese período para llevarse el triunfo. Miami pagó también sus problemas desde la línea de tiros libres, con catorce aciertos en veinticinco intentos. La mala noticia para los Mavericks fue la lesión de De Larrea, quien abandonó el encuentro tras disputar cinco minutos y cuarenta segundos, sin puntos y con un rebote. Dallas informó primero de que su regreso estaba en duda y posteriormente anunció que no volvería a jugar por una distensión en la rodilla derecha. articles.title: Dream star Angel Reese unhappy with officiating as WNBA Finals intensifies: 'A lot of us are getting fouled, and they're not calling it'
articles.summary: The third-year Defensive Player of the Year said she was frustrated after seeing her teammates "getting slapped to the ground or goggles knocked off" during...
articles.body:
SAN FRANCISCO — Angel Reese took aim at the lack of foul calls after the Atlanta Dream dropped Game 5 on Monday night , putting their backs against the wall in their chase for the franchise's first WNBA championship.

"We went up 2-1 and things shifted," Reese said. "I don't know what happened, but it definitely took a big turn."

The Dream dominated in back-to-back double-digit wins to go up in the series, but have now lost two consecutive games after falling to the Golden State Valkyries 64-55 at Chase Center. The Valkyries can win their first championship Thursday in Atlanta.

The third-year Defensive Player of the Year said she was frustrated seeing her teammates "getting slapped to the ground or goggles knocked off." She said the last game Valkyries forward Gabby Williams pulled her on purpose, and Reese screamed "foul" at the ref, but the crew didn't call it.

"A lot of us are getting fouled, and they're not calling it or we're talking to the ref after and they're saying, 'Oh, we'll get you next time,'" Reese said.

Reese is 4 of 20 from the field for 15 points over the last two games after scoring a combined 51 in the two victories. Her free-throw numbers have held steady throughout all five games, with the exception of a series-high 11 attempts in Game 2. She's 25 of 33 from the line in the series.

She continues to struggle against Valkyries center Kiah Stokes, who has set the Finals record for blocks (17) this series. After going without a field goal in the second half of Game 1, Reese said she wasn't aggressive enough. When asked again after the Game 4 loss about Stokes, Reese said it wasn't the defense but that she was rushing shots. She said she is still trying to figure out "how to play through the physicality," but that she's "used to it because it's just happening throughout the season."

"We'll figure it out," Reese said. "We're gonna have to just continue to push through the physicality and hopefully it goes our way next game."

Dream coach Karl Smesko credited the Valkyries' solid defense throughout the series, just as he had after Game 4, and noted his team's lackluster offensive performances.

"But I do want to have Angel's back here," Smesko said Monday. "The contact they allow on Angel compared to everybody else is just ridiculous, just ridiculous, and we should have gone to the foul line six to eight times more just on that."

Game 5 was the most even of the series at the free-throw line. Atlanta shot 11 of 14 and Golden State shot 10 of 13. But the gap is massive through the five games. Atlanta leads in free-throw attempts, 130-78, including a 35-19 differential in Game 2.

The WNBA postseason is notoriously known for its physical play. Neither side knocked the officiating until Monday night. In the previous two Finals, it had permeated its way through most of the playoffs. The league initiated an officiating task force in the offseason with a focus on freedom of movement.

It also hasn't been a smooth offensive series. Only once has a team shot better than 40% in a game. The Dream were 49.3% from the floor in the 97-71 Game 3 win. They shot a series-low 29.2% in Game 5.

"There's things that are on us; we're missing shots that we should make," Smesko said. "At the same time, that needs to be a whole lot better than it was. And it's time that if you push somebody with two hands as they drive, it's got to be a foul. I'm kind of tired of some of the excuses that I'm hearing."

Valkyries head coach Natalie Nakase was not told what was said by Reese during her post-game press conference, but was asked her thoughts on the physicality in the series.

"Finals. It's Finals. Yeah, this is it," Nakase said. "Both teams really want to win this. And, like you guys even said from the beginning of the Finals, this is two defensive-minded teams. So what are two defensive-minded teams? They like physicality. So that's part of it.

You guys act like I'm shocked. I ain't shocked about this. You have an Atlanta Dream team that's well coached that have dogs. I mean, same as us, and so yeah, it's part of it."

images.caption: Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream struggled once again in Game 5 on Monday night. (Ezra Shaw via Getty Images)

El español convirtió cuatro de sus seis lanzamientos de campo y tres de sus cuatro tiros libres, aunque también cometió cuatro pérdidas. Conectó cuatro de sus seis tiros de campo, incluido un triple, y Boston superó a Chicago por 34 puntos durante su presencia en pista. Cooper Flagg respondió con 29 puntos, seis rebotes, once asistencias, cuatro robos y dos tapones para los Mavericks, que también contaron con 20 puntos de P.J. Washington y 18 de Kyrie Irving.
