articles.title: Kiah Stokes goes beyond dirty work to power Valkyries to brink of WNBA title
articles.summary: The standout defender hit three 3-pointers to provide much-needed offense as Golden State moved one win away from its first championship.
articles.body:
SAN FRANCISCO — Head down. Blue-collar hoops.

Kiah Stokes heard it plenty over the past week from family and friends. She's a defensive specialist on the WNBA's best defensive team for a head coach rooted in defensive ideology.

Defense, defense, defense. Not that she needs any chanted reminder.

"I just know what I do," Stokes said. "A lot of my game isn't really pretty. I do the dirty work."

In what the Golden State Valkyries viewed as a must-win Game 5, she lifted her head up, dusted off her dormant skill and shot into Ballhalla's more glamorous stratosphere. The 6-foot-3 center scored a postseason-high 13 points on 6 field-goal attempts, shooting an eyebrow-raising 3 of 4 from 3-point range.

It was dirty work in a different way, grinding out the Valkyries' most efficient offensive game of the Finals. For the first time in five games, they cracked 39% from the floor — that is what constitutes a solid day in this defensively fueled battle. They're one win away from a WNBA championship in the expansion team's second season. Earlier in the day, the league announced Game 6 will be held at State Farm Arena in downtown Atlanta on Thursday with an earlier 12:30 p.m. ET (9:30 a.m. PT) tip time. The NBA's Hawks will host the Cavaliers at 8 p.m. ET at the arena.

For all the outside noise around when and where a potential clincher would be held, the Valkyries remained steady all day that they were focused on winning Game 5. They still hadn't proven their return to their characteristic style predicated on defense and valuing possessions would carry into another game. They were on their heels after back-to-back losses, and though a Game 4 win evened the series, Stokes knew it didn't win it.

Stokes tries to stay off social media, which is probably for the best. There is no glazing of her there, despite three WNBA championship rings as a starter. No, she's spent the majority of her career glazed over. While A'ja Wilson wanted to share her Defensive Player of the Year trophy and head coach Becky Hammon sang her praises in Las Vegas, Stokes' defensive input went largely unappreciated.

Most often, criticism mounted that she was an offensive liability. In this era of the game, one must do both. The move to Golden State, desperate for buckets, drew ire.

"Everyone wants to talk about the defense with Kiah," said Veronica Burton, who scored 13 on a less efficient 5-of-15. "But it's offense too."

It's not that Stokes is incapable. It's that she doesn't need to be a putback machine or a three-level scoring threat the way Liberty forward Jonquel Jones roams or Dream forward Angel Reese is developing. The 11-year veteran made it this far doing all the rest. On the eve of Game 1, she felt validated that this Finals shaped up as the league's best defenses in a year of historic offensive output.

She added 8 rebounds, 1 assist and 3 blocks in Game 5, an extension of the dominant defense she's played throughout the series. Again on Monday, she limited Reese and thereby stymied the rest of a team that carries a more potent offense than her own squad. That is standard.

She's on a run of six straight games with at least three blocks, tying two-time Los Angeles Sparks champion Lisa Leslie's 2003 run. With 17 blocks, she set the WNBA Finals record. And it's a clean mark doing it in five games, which was the previously used format that changed to seven last year. This is the first time the WNBA Finals will need a Game 6.

The first points of the game were scored by Stokes on an offensive putback. Later in the quarter, she missed a 3-point attempt. Any points were hard to come by.

Stokes makes those shots more than she misses in pregame warmups. One by one around the world they fall from the perimeter. She felt good about it in Game 4, but went 0 of 2 from 3. The Valkyries still won.

"It doesn't necessarily translate to the game because I don't shoot a lot," Stokes said. "I'm just really trying to just lean into it."

It helps when a teammate is honest, at least how head coach Natalie Nakase views such events.

She cussed. Tiffany Hayes cussed, angry her big gave up another open opportunity on a team that desperately needs all the offense it can acquire.

"I didn't want to make her mad again," Stokes said.

She made her next three, finishing with a career-high three 3-pointers on four attempts. The three-time UConn national champion didn't hit a 3-pointer in a WNBA game until her fifth season in the league. In six of her 11 seasons, she made three or fewer 3s. In only two, including this year, did she make at least 20 in the regular season.

"Now [she's] just shooting that 3-ball like it's a layup," said Nakase, who coached Stokes as an assistant in Las Vegas. "It was beautiful."

To win a championship requires unreal performances, and Stokes heard about it as time wound down on her home court.

"This is how we feel we can win it, and more importantly, Kiah Stokes will be our MVP," Nakase said. "I heard chants. I heard Kiah tonight."

The decibel-shattering crowd drowned out the broadcast interview with Stokes at center court. At every additional bellow, Stokes smiled slightly and waved it away in clear embarrassment. She's not one who likes the attention, as Nakase pointed out hours before tipoff.

articles.title: ‘So Embarrassing,’ ‘Unmitigated Disaster’ — Basketball World Rips WNBA As ESPN Insider Reveals Championship Ceremony May Be Held on ‘Practice Court’
articles.summary: The WNBA is drawing criticism after ESPN insider Ramona Shelburne reported Monday that the championship celebration could be moved to a practice court if the...
articles.body:
The WNBA is drawing criticism after ESPN insider Ramona Shelburne reported Monday that the championship celebration could be moved to a practice court if the Golden State Valkyries win the title in Game 6.

The possibility stems from a scheduling conflict at Atlanta's State Farm Arena, where an NBA game is set for later that day. Shelburne's report on "NBA Today" prompted sharp reactions from the basketball world.

Basketball Community Slams WNBA Over Potential Practice Court Celebration

Game 6 of the WNBA Finals is scheduled for Thursday at 12:30 p.m. ET, with the Atlanta Hawks hosting the Cleveland Cavaliers at State Farm Arena at 8 p.m.

The tight turnaround between the two games has raised concerns about how much time the arena will have to accommodate both events. Shelburne addressed the scheduling issue:

"That championship celebration may not actually be on that court," she said . "I've heard there are discussions about whether there's enough time to turn the arena over in time for the fans to celebrate on the court. It could be moved to like a practice court."

The possibility of moving the ceremony away from the main court drew criticism from across the basketball world.

Celtics writer Noa Dalzell posted , "This is ridiculous."

One WNBA observer raised concerns about what the arrangement could mean for the players, writing, "This is so embarrasing just potentially ruining a championship celebration."

Golden State leads the best-of-seven series 3-2 after defeating Atlanta 64-55 in Game 5 on Monday. The Valkyries can secure their first championship with another victory Thursday, while the Dream must win to force Game 7.

Reporter Kenzo Fukuda was equally critical of the potential arrangement for the ceremony.

"It's an unmitigated disaster that we've gotten to this point," he tweeted .

Pro Football Network also reacted : "So unserious."

The Athletic writer Stewart Mandel called the situation a "clown show," while also admitting that, despite his criticism, he selfishly hoped the series would return to the arena for Game 7 regardless of which team won.

NBA podcaster Joe Dellera expressed a familiar reaction in the discussion. "I cannot get over how absolutely ridiculous this entire thing is. Next level unserious behavior by the W."

One user took a sarcastic approach to the potential arrangement, posting , "'Lets make them celebrate in the back on the loading dock'- WNBA."

Shelburne's report concerned discussions about a possible move, not a finalized plan. Whether the league needs an alternative location for the celebration will depend first on Thursday's result.

articles.title: ANGEL REESE IS CARRYING THE WNBA ON HER BACK, BUT THE HATERS STILL REFUSE TO GIVE HER CREDIT
articles.summary: Angel Reese could win Defensive Player of the Year, rewrite the WNBA record book and help lead the Atlanta Dream to the Finals — and somehow, the conversatio...
articles.body:
Angel Reese could win Defensive Player of the Year, rewrite the WNBA record book and help lead the Atlanta Dream to the Finals — and somehow, the conversation would still find a way to criticize her.

At some point, the basketball has to matter more than the discourse.

Reese just completed a historic regular season. She led the WNBA with 12.1 rebounds per game, recorded a league-record 32 double-doubles and became the first player in league history to collect 500 rebounds in a single season.

She also earned Defensive Player of the Year and All-WNBA Second Team honors.

And yet, the debate around her game never seems to stop.

THE NUMBERS ARE GETTING IMPOSSIBLE TO IGNORE

Reese's impact goes far beyond highlight clips and social media arguments.

She set single-season WNBA records for total rebounds and offensive rebounds. Her relentless work on the glass creates extra possessions, gives Atlanta second chances and forces opposing defenses to account for her every time a shot goes up.

She also helped the Dream reach their first Finals since 2013.

That is not a small accomplishment. It is the result of a player whose production, rebounding and defensive presence have become central to a championship contender.

Atlanta did not trade for Reese to generate headlines. The Dream brought her in because she could help them win basketball games.

The Finals have already shown both sides of Reese's game.

She exploded for 30 points and 16 rebounds in Atlanta's Game 2 victory. Two nights later, she posted 21 points and 12 rebounds as the Dream routed Golden State 97-71.

Those performances helped put Atlanta ahead in the series and showed what happens when Reese finds her rhythm around the basket.

She was not simply collecting rebounds. She was scoring efficiently, finishing through contact and making life miserable for the opposing defense.

Golden State deserves credit for adjusting. But Reese has already demonstrated that she can take over a Finals game.

One difficult stretch does not erase that.

THE CRITICISM IS PART OF THE STORY — BUT IT ISN'T THE WHOLE STORY

Reese has never been a perfect player. Her finishing, shot selection and turnovers can become problems, particularly against a disciplined defense.

She acknowledged that herself after Game 4, when she scored eight points on 2-of-12 shooting in Atlanta's loss.

That honesty matters. Great players have to identify weaknesses and improve them.

But criticism becomes lazy when it ignores everything a player does well. Reese is an elite rebounder, an award-winning defender and a key piece of a team playing for a championship.

She does not need to be flawless to deserve recognition.

And she does not need to win every argument online to prove her value on the court.

Here is the uncomfortable truth for people who insist on treating Reese as a walking debate topic: Her résumé is growing regardless of what anyone posts about her.

She is a three-time All-Star, a Defensive Player of the Year and an All-WNBA selection. She has helped transform Atlanta into a legitimate championship contender.

At 24, she still has plenty of room to develop her offensive game and become an even more complete player.

That should excite basketball fans, not give them another excuse to dismiss what she has accomplished.

The Dream now trail Golden State 3-2 in the Finals after Monday's 64-55 loss. Reese scored seven points and grabbed 15 rebounds, and Atlanta faces elimination in Game 6.

The challenge is enormous. But if the Dream are going to force a deciding game, they need the version of Reese who dominates the glass and changes the game on both ends.

Angel Reese is not above criticism. She is above being reduced to it.

Give her credit for the historic season, acknowledge where she must improve and let the basketball tell the story.

Is Angel Reese already one of the most influential players in the WNBA — or will she have to win a championship before everyone finally gives her the respect she deserves?

articles.title: ANGEL REESE HAS A HUGE PROBLEM AND THE VALKYRIES JUST EXPOSED IT ON THE WNBA’S BIGGEST STAGE
articles.summary: Angel Reese has spent the 2026 season proving she can dominate the glass. Now, the Golden State Valkyries are asking a different question: Can she consistent...
articles.body:
Angel Reese has spent the 2026 season proving she can dominate the glass.

Now, the Golden State Valkyries are asking a different question: Can she consistently punish a defense when it takes away her easiest looks?

That question has become the defining issue of the WNBA Finals.

After posting 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2 and 21 points and 12 rebounds in Game 3, Reese has struggled to find the same offensive rhythm. She scored eight points on 2-of-12 shooting in Game 4, then managed just seven points in Monday's 64-55 loss in Game 5.

Atlanta now trails 3-2 in the series. One more loss ends the Dream's championship hopes.

The Valkyries are not trying to outscore Atlanta in a shootout. They are making every possession difficult.

Kiah Stokes and Golden State's defense have worked to crowd Reese near the basket, contest her finishes and force Atlanta to execute elsewhere.

Reese averaged 25.5 points in Atlanta's two Finals victories, shooting 60.7% from the field. In the two losses before Game 5, she averaged 11 points while shooting just 30.4%.

That is a massive difference for a player who has become one of the Dream's primary offensive engines.

Golden State has shown that containing Reese can change the entire game.

THE REBOUNDING IS ELITE. THE SCORING MUST FOLLOW.

Nobody can reasonably question Reese's ability to rebound.

She led the WNBA with 12.1 boards per game during the regular season and established league records for total rebounds, offensive rebounds and double-doubles.

Even in Game 5, she grabbed 15 rebounds.

But in a championship series, rebounding alone may not be enough. Atlanta needs Reese to convert more of those opportunities into points and make Golden State pay for loading up around the paint.

Her finishing has been inconsistent, and the Valkyries have made it difficult for her to establish comfortable looks.

That is not a reason to write her off. It is a challenge she must solve.

The best players find ways to adjust when opponents take away their strengths.

Atlanta's offensive struggles have not been limited to missed shots.

The Dream committed 17 turnovers in their Game 4 loss, and Golden State continued to capitalize on mistakes in Game 5. The Valkyries won the points-off-turnovers battle 21-6 on Monday.

When Atlanta gives away possessions, Reese and her teammates have fewer chances to establish their offense.

The solution cannot simply be to force-feed Reese the ball and hope for a different result. Atlanta needs cleaner possessions, better spacing and smarter decisions when Golden State sends help.

Reese also has to be decisive. If the defense collapses, she must recognize when to attack and when to move the ball.

Those are the adjustments championship teams have to make.

THIS IS THE MOMENT THAT WILL DEFINE HER FINALS

Reese deserves credit for helping Atlanta reach this stage. Her regular-season accomplishments are historic, and her performances in Games 2 and 3 showed just how dangerous she can be.

But the Finals are about responding when the opponent adjusts.

Golden State has won two straight games and is now one victory away from its first WNBA championship. Atlanta needs a response on Thursday.

Reese does not have to score 30 points again. She does have to become a more reliable offensive threat, protect the ball and make Golden State pay for its defensive attention.

Otherwise, the Valkyries will keep daring Atlanta to find another answer.

The real question is not whether Angel Reese can rebound. We already know she can. Can she adjust when the championship is on the line?

Is Golden State exposing a genuine weakness in Reese's offensive game, or is this simply a great defense making life difficult for a young star?

articles.body: Roberto Iñiguez, entrenador del Spar Girona de la Liga Femenina Endesa, se despachó a gusto en su cuenta de X (Twitter) contra sus críticos y los de su equipo. "Es gracioso cómo en malos momentos salen los de siempre, de los sitios de siempre y los coaches frustrados, resentidos, cuyo único refugio acabó siendo Twitter", apuntó el técnico vitoriano. Roberto Iñiguez se despidió con un mensaje contundente: "Mucha suerte; a todo el Staff y a las jugadoras nos importa un pepino lo que penséis. Todo lo contrario, sois gasolina". El Spar Girona que entrena Roberto Iñiguez ha empezado la temporada en la Liga Femenina Endesa con un balance de 1 victoria y 4 derrotas.
